passages.happening:
Five days later the high priest Ananias comes down to Caesarea with some elders and a lawyer named Tertullus, who sets out their case against Paul before the governor (verse 1).

Tertullus begins with praise. “Because of you, we have enjoyed a lasting peace, and your foresight has brought improvements to this nation” (verse 2). He promises to be brief (verses 3-4). Then the charges: “We have found this man to be a pestilence, stirring up dissension among the Jews all over the world. He is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes” (verse 5). He even tried to desecrate the temple, so they seized him (verse 6). If Felix examines him, he will learn that all this is true (verse 8). The Jews who have come with Tertullus agree that the charges are true (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Tertullus was a professional speaker hired for the case, someone who knew how a Roman court liked to be addressed. His speech follows the usual pattern of the time: praise for the judge to win his goodwill, a promise to be short, and then the charges.

The praise is flattery. Felix had put down bandits and rebels, so there was a little truth in ‘lasting peace’, but his rule was harsh and the province was growing more restless every year. The next note says more about him.

The charges are chosen for a Roman ear. A ‘pestilence’ who stirs up trouble ‘all over the world’ sounds like a threat to public order, which Rome punished hard. ‘Ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes’ makes the followers of Jesus of Nazareth sound like a faction. And the temple charge was the most dangerous of all: the notices at the temple barrier warned that a foreigner who passed it would die, and to bring one in was, in Jewish eyes, a grave crime.

Your Bible may have no verse 7. In some later manuscripts verses 6 to 8 are longer: they add that the Jews wanted to judge Paul by their own law, but the commander Lysias came and took him away by force. The earliest manuscripts do not have these words, so most modern Bibles leave them out or put them in a footnote. Nothing in the faith depends on them.

‘The Jews concurred’ (verse 9) means the high priest and the elders who came with him. It does not mean the Jewish people; the note on Acts 13:42-47 sets out how this site reads such phrases.
passages.ot:
The Scriptures warn against the smooth tongue. “A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet” (Proverbs 29:5). The Psalms pray against those who “speak with flattering lips and a double heart” (Psalm 12:2).

And God's law required real evidence before a man was condemned: “A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15). Tertullus brings words, not witnesses.
passages.asks: Tertullus praised a harsh ruler and painted an innocent man as a plague. Ask whether you are ever tempted to flatter people with power, or to describe someone you oppose in the worst possible light. And ask how you tell a well-made speech from a true one.

passages.t: Paul's defence: ‘the Way’, and the hope of resurrection
passages.happening:
Felix nods to Paul, and Paul begins: “Knowing that you have been a judge over this nation for many years, I gladly make my defense” (verse 10). Felix can check that it is no more than twelve days since he went up to Jerusalem to worship (verse 11). No one found him arguing in the temple or stirring up a crowd anywhere (verse 12), and they cannot prove their charges (verse 13).

But he does confess this: “I worship the God of our fathers according to the Way, which they call a sect. I believe everything that is laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets” (verse 14). He has the same hope in God as his accusers, “that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked” (verse 15). So he always tries to keep a clear conscience before God and people (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Paul's opening is courteous but plain. He does not flatter. He simply says he is glad to speak before a judge who knows the nation.

Then he answers with facts that could be checked. He had been in Jerusalem only twelve days. He came to worship. He started no argument and no riot. That was the heart of a defence in any court: where are the witnesses, and where is the proof?

And then, instead of only denying, he confesses. Yes, he belongs to ‘the Way’, the early name for the followers of Jesus, which his accusers call a ‘sect’, a breakaway party. But he worships ‘the God of our fathers’, the God of Israel. He believes the whole Law and the Prophets. He has not left Israel's faith. In his eyes, following Jesus is what Israel's faith was always pointing to.

His hope is the resurrection ‘of both the righteous and the wicked’. Many Jews in his day, the Pharisees above all, hoped that God would raise the dead at the end of the age. Paul says that hope includes everyone: all will be raised, and all will stand before God. That is why he tries to keep a clear conscience. A man who expects to give an account to God lives differently.
passages.ot:
The resurrection of the righteous and the wicked is Daniel's hope: “And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2). Ecclesiastes ends on the same note: “For God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil” (Ecclesiastes 12:14).

‘The God of our fathers’ is the name God gave himself at the burning bush (Exodus 3:15), and ‘the Law and the Prophets’ is Paul's way of naming the Scriptures of Israel, the Old Testament.
passages.asks: Paul denied what was false and confessed what was true, even when the truth was the very thing he was accused of. Ask whether you can be that plain about your faith when it costs something. And Paul lived with a clear conscience because he expected to stand before God. Ask how the hope of the resurrection, and the judgment, shapes the way you live this week.

passages.t: Alms for his people, and the missing accusers
passages.happening:
Paul tells what really happened. After several years away, he came to Jerusalem “to bring alms to my people and to present offerings” (verse 17). When they found him in the temple he was ceremonially clean, with no crowd and no uproar (verse 18).

“But there are some Jews from the province of Asia who ought to appear before you and bring charges, if they have anything against me” (verses 18-19). Or let the men here say what crime the council found in him (verse 20), unless it was the one thing he shouted: “It is concerning the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you today” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
‘Alms for my people’ is the only place in Acts that mentions the great collection Paul had gathered from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem. His letters speak of it often (Romans 15:25-28; 1 Corinthians 16:1-4). He had come not to attack his nation but to bring a gift to it.

And he had been ‘ceremonially clean’ in the temple: he was there for the purification and offerings of the vow (21:26). The man accused of defiling the temple was keeping its rules.

Then he makes a sharp legal point. The men who started the riot were ‘some Jews from the province of Asia’. Where are they? As the next governor will say, it was not the Roman custom to hand a man over before he had faced his accusers (25:16). Their absence was a real weakness in the case. Paul names them as particular people from one province, not as a people; the note on Acts 13:42-47 sets out how this site reads such phrases.

Finally he turns the charge round. The only thing the council actually heard from him was a cry about the resurrection. Is that a crime?
passages.ot:
Care for the poor was part of Israel's law: “there will never cease to be poor in the land; that is why I am commanding you to open wide your hand to your brother and to the poor and needy in your land” (Deuteronomy 15:11).

And the Law required accusers to stand up in person and be tested: “both parties to the dispute must stand in the presence of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 19:17).
passages.asks: Paul came to Jerusalem with a gift for people who were suspicious of him, and ended up in chains. Ask whether you are willing to keep doing good to people who misjudge you. And notice Paul's calm insistence on the facts. Ask how you answer an accusation: with heat, or with the truth plainly told.

passages.happening: Felix, “who was well informed about the Way” (verse 22), adjourns the hearing. He says, “When Lysias the commander comes, I will decide your case” (verse 22). He orders the centurion to keep Paul under guard, but to give him some freedom and let his friends look after his needs (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Felix knew more than he let on. Luke says he was ‘well informed about the Way’. There were believers in Caesarea, among them Philip and his daughters (21:8-9) and, years before, Cornelius's household (Acts 10). Felix had probably heard of the followers of Jesus for years. His wife was a Jewish princess, as the next note says.

He can see the case is weak. The accusers have no witnesses, and the Roman commander's own letter said there was no charge deserving death or prison (23:29). The just thing would have been to set Paul free. Instead Felix says he will wait for Lysias. Luke never tells us that Lysias came, or that the case was decided.

Paul is held in a lighter form of custody. He is guarded, but his friends may visit him and bring him what he needs. Luke himself may have been among the friends; the ‘we’ of the story picks up again when Paul sails from Caesarea (27:1).
passages.ot:
Delay can be a way of doing injustice. The prophet Habakkuk cried out, “How long, O LORD, must I call for help but You do not hear” (Habakkuk 1:2), and the Law warned judges, “Do not deny justice or show partiality” (Deuteronomy 16:19).

Yet God was with Joseph in prison too: “the LORD was with him and extended kindness to him, granting him favor in the eyes of the prison warden” (Genesis 39:21).
passages.asks: Felix knew what was right and put it off. Ask whether there is something you know you should decide or do, and you are waiting for a more convenient moment. And notice the friends allowed to care for Paul. Ask whether there is someone in a hard place you could visit or help.

passages.happening:
Some days later Felix comes with his wife Drusilla, who is Jewish. He sends for Paul and listens to him speak about faith in Christ Jesus (verse 24). “As Paul expounded on righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened” (verse 25). He says, “You may go for now. When I find the time, I will call for you” (verse 25).

At the same time Felix hopes Paul will offer him a bribe, so he sends for him often and talks with him (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Antonius Felix governed Judea in the 50s. He had been a slave. He and his brother Pallas were freed, and Pallas rose to great power at the emperor's court; the Roman historian Tacitus suggests that Felix was protected by his brother's influence. Tacitus judged Felix harshly, saying in one famous line that he used the power of a king with the mind of a slave, given to every kind of cruelty and lust. The Jewish historian Josephus tells of his harsh rule against bandits and rebels, and says that Felix even arranged the murder of a former high priest, Jonathan. These are the verdicts of ancient writers, given here in our own words.

Drusilla was the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I, the king who died in Acts 12, and the sister of Agrippa II and Bernice, who appear in the next chapter. Josephus says she had been married to a king of Emesa in Syria, and that Felix persuaded her to leave him and marry him.

So think about who was in the room when Paul spoke about ‘righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment’. Righteousness: before a governor whose justice was for sale. Self-control: before a man who had taken another king's wife. The coming judgment: before a judge who would himself be judged. Paul does not flatter them. He tells them the truth they most need.

Felix is frightened, and then he puts it off: ‘When I find the time’. And he keeps calling Paul back, Luke says, because he hoped for a bribe. Luke says it plainly. Felix could listen to the gospel many times and still be thinking about money.
passages.ot:
Paul stands where the prophets stood, speaking to the powerful about their sin. Nathan told King David to his face, “You are that man!” (2 Samuel 12:7), after David had taken another man's wife.

The Law said plainly, “Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous” (Exodus 23:8). And the prophets called rulers to “act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8).
passages.hard: Felix was frightened, and then he waited for a better time that never came, as far as Acts tells us. This is one of the plainest warnings in the book. A person can hear the truth, feel its weight, and still put it off for comfort, money or pride. Luke does not tell us what became of Felix's soul, and these notes will not guess. But he lets the reader see how close a man can come and still turn away.
passages.asks: Felix was frightened by the word about judgment and then said, ‘You may go for now.’ Ask whether there is a truth God has pressed on you that you keep putting off for a more convenient time. And Paul spoke of self-control to a man who had little. Ask whether you would have the courage to say the hard thing to someone with power over you, and the humility to hear it said to you.

passages.happening: Luke closes the chapter in one sentence. “After two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And wishing to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Two years. Paul, an innocent man, sits in custody in Caesarea for two full years because a governor wanted a bribe and then wanted to please Paul's enemies as he left office.

‘Wishing to do the Jews a favor’ means the leaders who had brought the charges, the high priest and his circle, whose goodwill Felix needed. It is not a word about the Jewish people; the note on Acts 13:42-47 sets out how this site reads such phrases.

The date of the change of governors is debated. Most scholars place Festus's arrival between about AD 58 and 60, and some argue for a few years earlier. The two years are usually read as the length of Paul's custody in Caesarea.

Luke does not explain the delay, and it would be too easy to invent a tidy reason for it. The injustice was real. Felix knew the case was weak and left Paul there anyway. Luke does not call that good. What readers have noticed beside it is this. The Lord had promised that Paul would testify in Rome (23:11), not that he would get there quickly. Paul was not idle: he had visitors, and some scholars suggest he wrote letters from Caesarea, though most place his prison letters in Rome or Ephesus. And the pattern of Scripture is that God keeps his promises through delay and injustice, not always by removing them.
passages.ot: Joseph knew this kind of waiting. He was jailed for a crime he did not commit, and the cupbearer who promised to remember him forgot. “After two full years had passed”, Pharaoh dreamed, and Joseph was called out of prison (Genesis 41:1). The Psalms give words for the long wait: “How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1), and also, “My times are in Your hands” (Psalm 31:15).
passages.hard: A word of care. Some people reading this have been kept waiting by a system that is not fair: held without a hearing, a case that drags on for years, a decision put off by people who do not care. This chapter does not tell you that the waiting is good, or that you must be silent about the wrong. Paul spoke up for himself, plainly and with the facts, and Luke names Felix's injustice for what it was. If you are in a long wait like this, you are not forgotten by God. Please do not carry it alone. Share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor, or someone who can give you sound legal advice. If the strain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul waited two years for a justice that did not come, and the Lord's promise still stood. Ask what you are waiting for, and whether you can bring God both your complaint and your trust, as the Psalms do. And ask whether you are ever the one keeping someone else waiting, out of convenience or to please others.
